description: Orca lets you run a fleet of coding agents (e.g. Claude Code, Codex) with your own subscription. Available on desktop, mobile and remote runtime.

# CI runners

Default to free GitHub-hosted standard runners: the repository is public and the
Enterprise plan allows 1,000 concurrent jobs (50 macOS). Use Blacksmith only for:

- macOS packaging: adhoc, hourly, daily and `release-mac-build.yml`. Hosted
  `macos-15` cannot boot the packaged x64 terminal host that `afterPack` verifies.
- The adhoc Windows build (a developer is waiting).
- Hardware-sensitive performance benchmarks. Operation-count contracts
  (`performance-contracts.yml`) are not, and run hosted.

PR checks run entirely on hosted runners. Unit tests
run as 12 shards on `ubuntu-24.04-arm`, which match the old five 8-vCPU
Blacksmith shards; `ORCA_UNIT_FULL_SHARD_COUNT` tunes the count. Preflight (lint
and typecheck) also runs on hosted ARM: shards, packaging and the layout oracle
do not wait for it, so its slower runner stays off the gate's critical path.
The layout oracle and advisory e2e lanes run on `ubuntu-24.04`. Git
compatibility runs one Git version per hosted job: three lanes sharing one
4-vCPU runner pushed real-Git tests past their timeouts.

Everything else, including the hourly and daily Windows builds, template
qualification and node-server lanes, runs on hosted `ubuntu-*`, `macos-15` and
`windows-2022` images. Do not use paid GitHub
larger runners: they cost more than Blacksmith at every size and Enterprise
included minutes do not cover them.

On Blacksmith, small routing and reporting jobs use 2 vCPUs; most test jobs use
4; compilation and shared JavaScript builds use 8. Mac checks use the 6-vCPU
Apple Silicon runners, including adhoc and release Mac packaging.

Keep matrix platform keys separate from runner labels: platform keys select
native slots, architectures, cache identities, and upload conditions.

## Cache stores

Blacksmith redirects `actions/cache` to its own store ("Enabling Blacksmith
transparent cache"); GitHub-hosted jobs use the repository's Actions cache. The
stores do not share entries, so the warmers (`ci-cache-warmup*.yml`) seed each
identity in both pools. Native module keys include the OS image, so a hosted
`ubuntu-22.04` consumer needs a hosted `ubuntu-22.04` warm leg.

GitHub's Actions cache is capped at 10 GB per repository and evicts the least
recently used entries first. Seed shared caches from `main`; avoid per-PR saves
of large or single-use artifacts, and prefer the lookup-only and restore-only
patterns in `.github/actions`.

## Production signing

SignPath requires every job in the signing workflow to use GitHub-hosted runners,
including jobs inside reusable workflows. `release-cut.yml` therefore explicitly
passes `fast_runners: false` to template qualification and `runner: ubuntu-latest`
to dependency security and shared JavaScript compilation. Preserve these overrides
when changing shared defaults.

The production Mac build already runs on Blacksmith in the separately dispatched
`release-mac-build.yml`. Keep its exact-run identity checks and publication gates.
Moving more production work to Blacksmith requires another isolated workflow;
changing a runner label inside `release-cut.yml` breaks signing provenance.

## Platform exceptions

These stay on GitHub-hosted runners even where the policy above picks Blacksmith:

- Windows WSL and WSL2 tests retain GitHub runners: Blacksmith Windows runners do
  not support the required nested virtualization.
- Windows signing and its rehearsal retain GitHub runners for SignPath provenance.
- Intel Mac and Windows ARM qualification retain their native GitHub runners;
  Blacksmith does not offer these architectures.
- Windows desktop lifecycle tests retain their existing GitHub desktop images.
- Mac SSH hostile-host tests retain GitHub images because Blacksmith's shell
  initialization restores the toolchain PATH that these fixtures must hide.
- Linux libc qualification keeps its pinned manylinux and Alpine containers,
  regardless of the host runner pool.

The shared dependency installer preserves temporary login-shell homes on
Blacksmith Linux hosts. Container jobs skip this host-image adjustment.

Runner availability: <https://docs.blacksmith.sh/blacksmith-runners/overview>.
Signing requirements: <https://docs.signpath.io/trusted-build-systems/github>.

# Unit test input ownership

Unit selection remains advisory. Every PR still executes the full unit inventory.

`config/scripts/ci/unit-selection/dependency-graph/ci-unit-input-ownership.json` records reviewed indirect repository inputs. A record covers the entire local source closure reachable from its `file`, including type imports. It does not remove ordinary import edges. Other callers of an indirect reader retain their own conservative fallback.

- `inputs`: exact repository paths or directory prefixes ending in `/`. Directory ownership includes new files. Unknown, deleted, renamed and global inputs still select the full suite.
- `emptyEnv`: optional external input overrides that must be absent or empty for the declaration to apply.
- `sourceClosureSha256`: `unitInputSourceDigest` of the sorted path/content entries in the local import closure. Unresolved or ambiguous package-directory imports cannot qualify.
- `contextSha256`: fingerprint of locked dependencies and the selection policy and unit runner/setup source closures. Dependency, policy or shared-runtime changes invalidate earlier review.
- `reason`: what was reviewed and why these inputs are sufficient.

The transcript replay record owns its captured-fixture directories and rejects optional external transcript/addon overrides. The compiler census owns all source, configuration and test directories. Reviewed URL/data projections have no indirect repository inputs.

A missing, malformed, duplicated or stale record keeps the conservative behavior. Before updating fingerprints, review the changed source closure, dependency/runtime context and any indirect reads again. Regenerating a digest does not establish ownership. The graph exposes `ownershipContextSha256`; source digests use `unitInputSourceDigest` from `ci-unit-input-ownership.mjs`.

For an eligible plan, `ci-shards/unit-selection.json` lists `checkedInputOwners`. Full successful and failing references, input addition/deletion/rename cases and hosted timing evidence are required before changing execution policy. Omitted worker time overlaps across processes and must not be reported as runner savings.

# Worktree storage maintenance

Run one command from the repository to preview maintenance across its locally registered Git worktrees:

```sh
pnpm reclaim-space
```

In an interactive terminal, the preview offers `Apply this cleanup? [y/N]`; enter `Y` to apply it.
Redirected input or output remains preview-only. To apply without a prompt, use `pnpm reclaim-space --apply`.

Historical test checkouts inside a worktree are removed only when the worktree is idle for 7 days:
no running process references its path, HEAD has not moved, and no changed or untracked Git path
was modified. To include active worktrees too, stop cross-version tests in all this
repository's worktrees, then preview with:

```sh
pnpm reclaim-space --tests-stopped
```

Answer `Y` to apply that preview, or use `pnpm reclaim-space --apply --tests-stopped` to apply directly.

The command reuses the historical test cache, Electron distribution, dev bundle, and Vite cache cleanup scripts.
It shares complete Electron distributions through the repository cache and removes idle
`out/electron-dev` bundles, which development rebuilds on demand. It also removes tracked
`.cache/vite` dependency caches unused for 30 days. It also removes stamped historical test
checkouts and shared seeds older than 30 days; tests regenerate them when needed. It leaves source files,
worktree registrations and branches intact. Manual and automatic cleanup also include old dependency
installs and build output as described below. Reported sizes are
logical file data; APFS clones and hardlinks mean actual disk savings can be smaller.

Use `--release-cache-min-age-days 7` to shorten historical-cache retention, or `0` to select all
recognised completed historical checkouts. This age option applies only to test caches. Local
checkout age uses directory modification time, which ordinary reuse does not refresh. Shared seeds
are protected by the copy lease, so they need no flag. Older harnesses hold no lease while reading
a local checkout, so local checkouts are selected only from idle worktrees (as defined above;
ignored files such as agent tooling directories do not count, and an unreadable process table or
Git failure counts as active). `--tests-stopped` acknowledges stopped
tests and includes active worktrees; it does not detect running tests.
Cache cleanup skips symlinks, malformed stamps, future formats, and publication/copy locks.
See [release source sharing](./release-source-sharing.md) for the cache and locking details.

Vite dev servers record cache use at startup and shutdown. Cleanup retains recent caches,
caches owned by a live process, and caches whose ownership cannot be verified, including caches
created before tracking was added. A maintenance lock prevents cleanup racing with server startup.
Desktop and web caches are reclaimed together; the next dev launch regenerates them as needed.

Use `--repo DIRECTORY` to choose another local repository. Git's worktree list determines scope,
including registered worktrees outside Orca's workspace directory. Folder workspaces without Git
have no repository-wide sweep. These commands run on the local host: they do not inspect or delete
anything on SSH hosts. Run maintenance on the execution host when maintaining remote repositories.

## Old dependency installs and build output

Old generated files are included in the normal manual command and automatic dev cleanup:

```sh
pnpm reclaim-space
pnpm reclaim-space --apply
```

This pass retains the selected repository worktree, the invoking worktree, and any
`--exclude-worktree` directory. It removes ignored, completely untracked `node_modules`, `out`,
`dist`, and `build` directories older than 30 days. Recognized package roots are the repository
root, `mobile`, `native/*`, `src/packages/*`, `cloud/apps/*`, and `cloud/packages/*`, each with a
regular `package.json`. It does not search arbitrary folders or the user's home directory.
Use `--generated-min-age-days 14` to shorten retention, or `0` to include recent generated
directories. Age is the directory modification time, not proof that an install is unused.
Old sibling installs and output can be removed while sibling work is running; reinstall
dependencies or rebuild in that worktree if needed. Shared pnpm package data is retained.

Preview leaves files in place. Apply rechecks Git tracking, parent paths, directory identity
and modification time before deleting. Symlinked directories, symlinked package parents, nested
repositories and directories containing tracked files are retained. Read-only generated
directories can be made writable for removal; hardlinked package files are never chmodded.
Source files, local changes, worktree registrations, branches, and shared pnpm stores remain
intact. Generated files are recreated by installing dependencies or rebuilding in that worktree.
APFS clones and hardlinks mean directory sizes can greatly overstate the actual space reclaimed.

Machine-wide caches, Docker images/volumes, downloads and simulator data remain
outside this repository-scoped command.

## Keeping installs shared

Healthy Electron installs join the shared distribution cache during native dependency setup,
without waiting for an Electron upgrade. The manual command migrates older installs immediately.
Read-only Electron package directories are retained and reported as skipped. Cache publication
or copying failures are also reported as skipped rather than silently omitted.

`pnpm dev` and `pnpm dev-stable-name` start an automatic repository-wide cleanup worker for
Electron, Vite caches, old dependency installs and generated output, and per-worktree dev
profiles whose worktree was removed (a profile is kept while its app, runtime, or terminal daemon
is still running),
in the background after the dev process starts. It never prompts or waits before launching the app.
The worktree being launched is excluded from every pass except historical test caches, which use
the idle-worktree rule. Existing bundle checks protect
active sibling Electron bundles and recent unfinished bundles from the bundle-specific pass;
the generated-directory pass uses its 30-day age cutoff and filesystem/Git protections.
Background sweep output is suppressed; worker start or exit failures are reported without stopping dev. Set `ORCA_SKIP_DEV_STORAGE_RECLAIM=1` to opt out.
The worker finishes independently if the dev app exits, and each cleanup operation has a ten-minute limit.

Automatic invocations also run historical test cache cleanup with the idle-worktree rule; they
never pass `--tests-stopped`, so active worktrees keep their local checkouts.
The repository lock prevents competing cleanup commands. Dev bundle removal checks active
processes and recent unfinished builds, then rechecks eligibility immediately before deletion.
An unreadable process table prevents removal.

To retain older bundles during a manual sweep, run the underlying command with an age limit:

```sh
node config/scripts/worktree-storage/reclaim-dev-electron-bundles.mjs --min-age-days 7 --apply
```

That limit uses the bundle directory's modification time. The underlying command also accepts
`--exclude-worktree DIRECTORY` to protect an entire worktree. A missing exclusion path is an error;
filesystem aliases resolve to the same worktree. Neither option schedules cleanup.

"""Owned disposable-item setup for the Windows native replacement contract."""
import ctypes
import sys
from ctypes import wintypes

phase, target = sys.argv[1:]
assert target.startswith('orca-sta11846-test:') and target != 'gemini:antigravity'

class Attribute(ctypes.Structure):
    _fields_ = [('Keyword', wintypes.LPWSTR), ('Flags', wintypes.DWORD),
                ('ValueSize', wintypes.DWORD), ('Value', ctypes.POINTER(ctypes.c_ubyte))]

class Credential(ctypes.Structure):
    _fields_ = [('Flags', wintypes.DWORD), ('Type', wintypes.DWORD),
                ('TargetName', wintypes.LPWSTR), ('Comment', wintypes.LPWSTR),
                ('LastWritten', wintypes.FILETIME), ('CredentialBlobSize', wintypes.DWORD),
                ('CredentialBlob', ctypes.POINTER(ctypes.c_ubyte)), ('Persist', wintypes.DWORD),
                ('AttributeCount', wintypes.DWORD), ('Attributes', ctypes.POINTER(Attribute)),
                ('TargetAlias', wintypes.LPWSTR), ('UserName', wintypes.LPWSTR)]

api = ctypes.WinDLL('advapi32', use_last_error=True)
api.CredReadW.argtypes = [wintypes.LPCWSTR, wintypes.DWORD, wintypes.DWORD,
                         ctypes.POINTER(ctypes.POINTER(Credential))]
api.CredReadW.restype = wintypes.BOOL
api.CredWriteW.argtypes = [ctypes.POINTER(Credential), wintypes.DWORD]
api.CredWriteW.restype = wintypes.BOOL
api.CredFree.argtypes = [ctypes.c_void_p]

if phase == 'seed':
    prior = ctypes.POINTER(Credential)()
    assert not api.CredReadW(target, 1, 0, ctypes.byref(prior))
    assert ctypes.get_last_error() == 1168
    blob = (ctypes.c_ubyte * 7)(*b'initial')
    value = (ctypes.c_ubyte * 3)(1, 2, 3)
    attributes = (Attribute * 1)(Attribute('orca-fixture', 0, 3, value))
    credential = Credential(0, 1, target, 'fixture-comment', wintypes.FILETIME(),
                            7, blob, 1, 1, attributes, 'fixture-alias', 'fixture-user')
    assert api.CredWriteW(ctypes.byref(credential), 0), ctypes.get_last_error()
elif phase == 'verify':
    raw = ctypes.POINTER(Credential)()
    assert api.CredReadW(target, 1, 0, ctypes.byref(raw)), ctypes.get_last_error()
    try:
        credential = raw.contents
        assert (credential.Type, credential.Flags, credential.Persist) == (1, 0, 1)
        assert (credential.UserName, credential.Comment, credential.TargetAlias) == (
            'fixture-user', 'fixture-comment', 'fixture-alias')
        assert credential.AttributeCount == 1
        attribute = credential.Attributes[0]
        assert (attribute.Keyword, attribute.Flags) == ('orca-fixture', 0)
        assert ctypes.string_at(attribute.Value, attribute.ValueSize) == bytes([1, 2, 3])
        assert ctypes.string_at(credential.CredentialBlob, credential.CredentialBlobSize) == b'replacement-fixture'
    finally:
        api.CredFree(raw)
else:
    raise AssertionError('unknown fixture phase')

# Computer-use task benchmark

Compares Orca's direct Linux AT-SPI and Windows UI Automation providers with
cua-driver 0.38.0. This does not measure the CLI, sidecar, model, or complete agent
workflows. It does not install cua-driver in Orca.

Run the `Computer-use task benchmark` GitHub Actions workflow on a branch. Native
input runs only on its disposable Windows runner or Linux Xvfb desktop. The runner
refuses to run on the developer's desktop. Keep `ORCA_BACKGROUND_LAUNCH=1`.

The first matrix covers GTK/WinForms and Electron fixtures. Editor applications,
Wayland, macOS and additional Windows control frameworks need separate coverage.
Do not generalize these results to every application on a platform.

## Measurement contract

- Baseline and candidate runtimes come from full commit SHAs, copied before the
  run. Artifacts include source hashes, cua executable hash/version, image,
  seed, complete trial plan, responses, snapshots and independent fixture states.
- Each individual trial launches a fresh target, sentinel and provider. Process
  groups on Linux and jobs on Windows contain children, including timed-out calls.
  The provider is terminated and reaped before the terminal oracle read. No retry
  follows an uncertain mutation.
- Reset carries a unique nonce bound to the fixture instance and PID. The fixture
  acknowledges after applying text, selection, logical focus, counters, combo,
  scroll and menu state. Sentinel foreground and stacking are independently checked.
- Invalid preparation executes no provider operation, is excluded from the scored
  denominator, and makes the run incomplete with nonzero exit status. A missing or
  ambiguous control after valid setup is a scored coverage failure.
- Strict selectors require a unique matching role and label. References are fresh
  before the task and after every step. There is no label-only or role-only fallback.
- Completion requires exact independent final state, including unchanged decoy text
  and exactly one click/submit. Submission handlers capture the submitted text;
  Increment handlers capture the selected color at click time. Submit tasks require
  the marker in the submission, and choose-and-click requires Blue at the click.
  Final text/color alone cannot prove those events carried the intended values.
  Raw text is never cleaned. API errors, missing final
  observations and observed interference remain separate from task completion.
- The observer starts before provider initialization and initial selector snapshot,
  and stays active through all steps, reads, shutdown and settling. No sentinel
  refocusing happens during measurement. Idle and deliberate-steal controls must pass.
- Complete tasks run without simulated user typing. Separate click and scroll probes
  type `q` into the sentinel. Event counters preserve evidence even if agent input
  selects or deletes text. Observations sample roughly every 4 ms; they cannot prove
  the absence of shorter focus/pointer/clipboard changes. X11 clipboard observations
  detect ownership changes, not all changes made by the same owner.
- Engine order rotates across rounds from a recorded seed. Use a multiple of three
  rounds for balanced positions. Default/background and explicitly requested
  foreground profiles are separate trials. Foreground can intentionally interfere.
- Comparable per-step time includes the action and an additional full no-screenshot
  observation for every provider. Raw action time is diagnostic because Orca already
  returns a snapshot with mutations. Task time includes provider startup, discovery
  and all action/read pairs. Medians include completed tasks only; failed-attempt
  durations and sample counts are separate. Diagnostic serialization and disk I/O
  happen after timing. Final independent readback after shutdown is an upper
  bound on effect time, recorded separately.
- Fatal errors, invalid setup, failed observers, unobserved completion, budget
  exhaustion or missing planned cells leave JSON evidence and exit nonzero. A valid
  observed task failure remains a benchmark result, not an infrastructure failure.

Tasks cover explicit text targeting with another field logically focused, Unicode
entry plus submit, select-all replacement plus submit, and color choice plus one
click. Interference probes remain separate from task latency comparisons.

Explicit-target typing is a native capability probe. Orca's public CLI/RPC currently
accepts typing at the focused field and does not expose an element target for text.
Failure of this probe identifies a capability to consider adding; it does not prove
a violation of the current public typing contract. Click-then-type tasks exercise
the existing sequence, although this benchmark still bypasses public transports.

The Linux Electron job also records restoration stages in `focus-probe/results.json`.
It records the AT-SPI focus acknowledgment, selected ACTIVE state, manual legacy PID
fallback, managed/native IDs, explicit singleton activation, minimized restoration
and the candidate's behavior with two same-PID windows. Managed windows include
minimized windows and exclude unmanaged helper windows.
The primary fixture publishes its native ID, checked against its PID before the probe.
Probe success establishes restoration behavior; actual text-and-submit completion
comes from the separate task results above.

AT-SPI ACTIVE is the runtime's focus authority. Global input can still race a later
focus change, and singleton accessibility/native counts do not establish an atomic
identity mapping if a window closes or the accessibility tree is stale. The probe
covers stable fixtures and detected ambiguity, not those concurrent lifecycle races.

## Headless contract checks

```sh
ORCA_BACKGROUND_LAUNCH=1 python3 -m unittest discover -s config/benchmarks/computer-use -p 'test_*.py'
```

These checks protect the historical false-success cases and process-tree cleanup.
They do not import desktop observers or generate native input.

Transports, fixtures and observers were adapted from the historical
`bench/computer-cua` prototype at `68a68ccf0f16c0a7f952d55adfe21850247b8ee9`.
Historical checkouts and result artifacts remain unchanged.

# Native chat tool pairing

Latest follow-up: [mobile row identity](./mobile-row-identity.md) keeps an opened detail with its command after earlier rows disappear or move.

Long tool runs repeatedly scanned all unanswered calls to find each named result.
Calls that emitted no output stayed at the front of that scan. Positional results
also shifted the remaining pending-call array after every answer.

The shared matcher now uses a linked FIFO and builds an ID index only when a
named answer needs to match beyond its head. That index stays valid until the
pending queue empties. Named and unnamed answers remove a pending call without
array movement; each call enters the index at most once. Duplicate IDs retain
FIFO order. Existing pair limits and output references are preserved.
The implementation remains shared by desktop, mobile, and host readers.

The rendered check exposed related correctness defects: Claude and Codex
transcript decoders discarded result IDs, and folding used only call counts to
assign results. Decoders now retain the optional provider ID; folding uses
the canonical matcher and occurrence indices, so an unrelated result cannot
consume another call's answer. Unmatched named results stay visible separately
and cannot acquire a guessed owner during later folds. Results without IDs
remain positional; already imported calls missing IDs cannot own named results.

Legacy journal import also preserves IDs on singleton calls and keeps singleton
results as result messages. The focused importer/projector regression test
covers reverse batched results, mixed record shapes, duplicate IDs, anonymous
FIFO, and old persisted calls whose IDs were already lost. That integration
coverage is separate from the rendered transcript fixture below.

## Reproduction and measurements

Baseline: `51e7181850b`. At 2,048 calls, the regression tests measured 2,098,176
ID reads for reverse completions, 4,194,304 reads for silent-call backlogs and
unmatched results, and 2,096,128 moved array slots for FIFO completions. The
fixed implementation passes linear operation budgets at 64, 512, and 2,048
calls. Semantic differential tests preserve call/result references across
mixed IDs, interleavings, immutable inputs, and unusual limits.

Run the production benchmark with the original module on stdin:

```sh
git show 51e7181850b:src/shared/native-chat-tool-fold.ts |
  ORCA_BACKGROUND_LAUNCH=1 node config/scripts/native-chat-tool-pairing-benchmark.mjs
```

[benchmark.json](./benchmark.json) records eight counterbalanced sample pairs
per workload, source bundle hashes, raw timings, and correctness checks. It
includes immediate pairs, reverse completion, positional FIFO, duplicate IDs,
silent-call backlogs, unmatched results, and finite limits at seven sizes.
At 2,048 calls, reverse completion improved from 7.46 ms to 0.163 ms, a
silent-call backlog from 13.02 ms to 0.244 ms, and immediate ordered pairs from
92.0 microseconds to 47.3 microseconds. Single-call backlog/missing workloads
remain within 11 ns of the baseline. These timings cover the shared pairing
function, not React, DOM, transport, or the full transcript projection. These
measurements identify the earlier matcher revision in the artifact. Later orphan
projection, journal import, and discarded-wrapper allocation changes are outside
this benchmark's scope.

The deterministic contract runs in `pnpm test:perf:contracts`. Broader coverage
uses the shared/native-chat and renderer/native-chat suites, provider transcript
reader suites, and `tests/e2e/native-chat-tool-pairing.spec.ts` for hidden
Electron rendering and output ownership.

## Full folding, allocation, and mobile disclosure

The later allocation fix reuses the same matcher for folding attribution without
collecting pair wrappers that folding immediately discarded. Consumer pairing
still returns fresh wrappers with the original call/result references. No cache,
parallel matcher, or ownership fallback was added.

Run the three-version production-module benchmark and its retained-allocation
control with:

```sh
ORCA_BACKGROUND_LAUNCH=1 node --expose-gc config/scripts/native-chat-fold-benchmark.mjs --memory-control
ORCA_BACKGROUND_LAUNCH=1 node --expose-gc config/scripts/native-chat-fold-benchmark.mjs
```

[full-fold-benchmark.json](./full-fold-benchmark.json) compares original
`51e7181850b`, published `b1e44269d655`, and the measured worktree. It records
54 cases across three sizes, six workloads, and full folding, settled desktop
projection plus all-row render-data pairing, and repeated folding. Each
comparison uses six counterbalanced sample pairs; the table uses raw-sample
medians because the artifact's rounded summary loses microsecond precision.
The two comparisons have separate current samples.

| All-row projection and pairing                     | Original → current               | Published → current |
| -------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| 8,192 reverse completions                          | 320.4727 → 3.7358 ms, about 86×  | 3.5954 → 3.6126 ms  |
| 8,192 silent calls plus 8,192 later answered calls | 558.9641 → 5.5075 ms, about 101× | 5.5551 → 5.2629 ms  |
| 8,192 immediate ordered pairs                      | 2.4124 → 2.5636 ms               | 2.6577 → 2.3606 ms  |

These are large adversarial-run gains, not a general frame-time improvement.
At 32 immediate pairs, the original/current pipeline medians were 11.38 and
16.74 microseconds: roughly 5.4 microseconds of extra work. The separate
published/current comparison measured 15.60 and 13.10 microseconds. Original
folding and refolding alone were faster than the ownership-preserving fold:
for the large silent backlog, folding rose from 1.1191 to 2.6317 ms and refolding
from 0.3171 to 1.4090 ms. The expensive original consumer scan dominates the
large named-result cases. Full folding still visits the collection on updates;
settled row reuse does not make the fold incremental.

Against published C, the large fold medians fell approximately 3–9%; whole
pipeline changes varied, including the small reverse-case increase above.
The deterministic allocation gain is clearer: large silent-backlog folding
collects zero discarded pair wrappers instead of 16,384, while consumer pairing
retains the required 16,384. Its median pre-GC heap delta fell from 8.23 to
6.84 MB; retained output stayed near 0.23 MB. Named orphan conservation,
original block references, unique row IDs, and repeated-fold identity are
checked for published/current outputs, which are deeply equal for every
workload. Original output counts expose historical drops or guessed ownership;
those cases do not provide equivalent visible-output timing comparisons.

Preserving separately sourced orphan evidence still costs rows and memory.
With 8,192 singleton orphan outputs, current folding retains roughly 2.61 MB
versus the original's 0.15 MB; fresh all-open projection and pairing retain
about 9.23 MB versus 0.33 MB. Published/current retention is essentially the
same. The original grouped these outputs with unrelated calls. Desktop
windowing normally mounts only viewport rows, while this consumer benchmark
processes every run as opened. It excludes React commits, DOM layout, mobile
runtime, and transport latency.

[full-fold-memory-control.json](./full-fold-memory-control.json) confirms that
the sampling method retains a live million-slot array at about 8 MB. Each
memory sample releases its preceding output, holds the current output through
forced GC, and excludes shared source inputs. Projection memory uses a fresh
projector/cache; timing reuses a settled projector. Pre-GC deltas indicate
allocation pressure, not peak memory or total allocated bytes. Negative
retained deltas are noise, not savings or per-update growth.
[full-fold-benchmark-receipt.json](./full-fold-benchmark-receipt.json) records
commands, source/tool hashes, and the post-main-merge graph review. Only three
account-startup enum/map modules changed after measurement; those branches are
absent from the benchmark fixtures, so no new timing claim is made for them.

Mobile previously exposed only six tool rows with no way to reach later
outputs. The existing disclosure now reveals six more rows per request and can
collapse back to six. A closed run performs no pairing; an opened run collects
only the requested prefix plus one sentinel to decide whether Show more is
available. This limits wrapper and mounted-row retention, while matching may
still scan a pending suffix to find the requested owners. Long runs require
multiple reveals, and expanding them mounts more rows at the user's request.
Result-only summaries use the existing Result label without inventing a call
count. Local mobile stream and SSH-authoritative handler tests cover late named
completion, orphan reachability, cursor paging, and older-host no-cursor
replacement. They establish ownership and paging behavior, not network latency.

## Rendered verification

The rebuilt Electron app passed the dedicated E2E test through the real Claude
JSONL reader: three reverse completions behind 32 silent calls, an unrelated
result, and successful/failed task updates. The [inspected screenshot](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/79f41dc6-8ec8-4f12-8e89-e4d7ec4b5daa)
shows all three outputs attached to their commands, the accepted pending task,
and the unrelated output under its own Result summary and row.
[rendered-validation.json](./rendered-validation.json) records the
commands, test source hash, exact worktree identity, hidden/unfocused native
window assertions, and process cleanup. The fixture uses synthetic Claude
JSONL through the production reader and real UI clicks. This is desktop
correctness evidence; it does not exercise an actual provider CLI or adoption
launch, measure mobile rendering, or measure SSH transport latency.

The mobile component check uses the actual React Native Web primitives and
production message/fold modules under the shipped browser build options and

# Hello Worker Panel

A components panel written in TSX with no build step, and the plugin's own worker. Start from
[hello-tsx](../hello-tsx) for a panel alone; this one adds everything a panel can reach beyond its
own UI, so it runs as a full-access (`trusted-worker`) plugin. Orca transpiles `src/*.tsx` and
`src/*.ts` when the panel loads (types stripped, JSX compiled for `orca`, relative imports such as
`./todos` resolved to their files).

```sh
orca plugin dev load .   # also writes .orca/types, the typings tsconfig.json extends
npx tsc -p .             # optional type check
```

Import only `orca` and relative files: there is no bundler, so `import 'react'` fails with an
error naming the file and the import.

It shows one of each part of the API:

- **Components**: keyed atoms, `derived` values, `setup(ctx)` and `ui.has` feature detection.
- **Panel → worker**: Suggest calls `plugin.request('tasks.suggest')`, answered by
  `orca.panels.handle` in `worker/main.mjs`, which starts on the panel's first request.
- **Worker → panel**: the worker `orca.panels.post`s `tasks.allDone` when the last task is done;
  the panel hears it with `plugin.on`.
- **Shared storage**: the task list is `atom('todos', ..., { persist: 'storage' })`, so the
  worker reads the same value with `orca.storage.get('todos')` and hears each change.
- **Settings**: `contributes.settings` declares `celebrate`, `suggestions` and `suggestionOrder` (a switch, a text box and a picker); change them under
  the plugin in Orca's Settings and the worker reads them with `orca.settings.get`.
- **Events**: `on('agent.status.changed')` counts working agents (the `agent:read` capability).
- **One typed contract**: `src/protocol.ts` declares `PluginRequests` and `PluginPanelEvents` in
  `declare module 'orca'`, so both sides type-check against it.

title: Race three agents on the same task
---

Running the same task across multiple agents in parallel is Orca's killer move. Same prompt, three branches, pick the winner.

## Steps

1. Create three worktrees from the same start-from ref. Name them `fix-bug`, `fix-bug-2`, `fix-bug-3`.
1. Launch a different agent in each — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor CLI.
1. Paste the same prompt into all three.
1. Watch the sidebar [status indicators](/docs/model/agents-sessions#state-indicators) and jump between worktrees with `Cmd-J` (macOS) / `Ctrl-Shift-J` (Windows / Linux) — each worktree keeps its own pane layout.
1. When they finish, review each diff. Use [Annotate AI Diff](/docs/review/annotate-ai-diff) on the winner.
1. Commit, push, open PR from the winning worktree.
1. Delete the two losers — one click removes the worktree and branch.

## Why it works

Different agents make different mistakes. Running the same task in parallel is cheaper than sequential retries and surfaces disagreement as a signal. Where three agents agree, the answer is probably right. Where they split, you've found the hard part.
